whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Technical Architect exam for?

personas.label: Senior Salesforce architects
personas.description: You already lead large implementations and want the credential that sits at the top of the Salesforce path.

personas.label: Consultancy practice leads
personas.description: You design multi-cloud solutions for enterprise clients and defend those designs to their executives.

personas.label: Long-term platform specialists
personas.description: You hold Application Architect and System Architect and are deciding whether to commit to the board.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Technical Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: Technical Architect is the hardest Salesforce credential, and it is not a multiple-choice exam. You hold both Application Architect and System Architect first, then take a two-stage assessment: a readiness evaluation, then a review board where you present a solution and defend it to judges.
bullets: Not a multiple-choice exam. You design a solution to a scenario and defend it live.
Two prerequisites. Application Architect and System Architect, which are themselves eight exams between them, seven of them unique.
Two stages. An architect evaluation first, then the review board.
Expensive. Third-party sources put the total around US$6,000 across both stages. Confirm current fees with Salesforce before committing.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Most successful candidates have run several large Salesforce programmes and have practised the format repeatedly with mock boards. Preparation is usually measured in months of rehearsal, not weeks of reading.

examFormat.heading: Technical Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: There is no multiple-choice CTA exam. Here is how the credential works:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Both stages are built around a hypothetical enterprise scenario: a company with existing systems, business goals, constraints and problems. You design the solution, then explain and defend it.
bestWayToPass: Finish the prerequisites first: Application Architect and System Architect must both be active before you can apply.
Practise defending, not reciting: Judges interrupt and challenge. Rehearse with people who will push back on your choices.
Answer the requirement you were given: Most failures are elegant designs that solve a different problem from the one in the scenario.
Be able to justify every box: If you put middleware on the diagram, be ready to say why, and what you rejected.

certificationCard.description: Technical Architect is Salesforce's top credential. It is awarded through a two-stage assessment rather than a multiple-choice exam: a readiness evaluation, then a review board where you present and defend an architecture for a hypothetical enterprise scenario.

keyConcepts.h2: Salesforce Technical Architect (CTA): Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: How the Credential Is Structured
blocks.body: CTA sits on top of the two role-based architect credentials. **Application Architect** is awarded for Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. **System Architect** is awarded for Platform Developer I, Integration Architect, Identity and Access Management Architect, and Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect. Platform Developer I counts toward both, so there are seven distinct exams to pass before CTA is open to you. After that come the two assessment stages, each with its own fee and its own booking.

blocks.heading: Stage One: The Architect Evaluation
blocks.body: The first stage is a readiness assessment with a Salesforce evaluator, built around a scenario. It exists to check that you are ready for the full board before you and Salesforce spend the time and money on it. You work through a scenario, produce a design, and discuss it. Passing this stage is what opens access to the review board. Treat it as a real attempt rather than a rehearsal: the skills it tests, reading a scenario accurately and justifying choices, are exactly the ones the board tests.

blocks.heading: Stage Two: The Review Board
blocks.body: In the review board you are given a scenario in advance, design a complete solution, then present it to a panel of judges who are themselves CTAs. The session covers your presentation and then extended questioning, where judges probe the weak points of your design. They are testing judgement under pressure: whether you understood the requirements, whether your design is justifiable, whether you know its risks, and whether you can adjust when challenged. The decision is the board's, based on how you cover the required areas rather than a percentage score.

blocks.heading: What the Judges Are Actually Looking For
blocks.body: Across both stages the same themes recur. **Requirement coverage:** every stated business requirement is addressed, and you can point to where. **Justification:** each significant choice has a reason, and you can name what you rejected and why. **Trade-offs:** you acknowledge the cost of your decisions rather than presenting a design as perfect. **Risk:** you can say what could go wrong and how you would mitigate it. **Communication:** a business audience could follow your explanation. Deep platform knowledge is assumed; it is the reasoning on top of it that is assessed.

blocks.heading: Preparing Realistically
blocks.body: Reading about architecture is not preparation for this format. Work from full scenarios, produce complete designs under time limits, and present them to people who will interrupt. Build a repeatable structure for your presentation so you cover data, security, integration, development lifecycle and licensing without having to remember. Record yourself and watch where you waffle. Most people who pass have sat several mock boards with practising CTAs, and most who fail at the board have never been challenged out loud before the day.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Certified Technical Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Preparation for CTA is practice, not revision. These are the areas where candidates most often lose marks.

blocks.heading: Justify Every Decision
blocks.body: For each component on your diagram, be ready to say why it is there and what you considered instead. An unexplained box is a question waiting to be asked.

blocks.heading: Trade-offs, Not Perfection
blocks.body: Every design costs something. Name the downside of your choice before a judge does, and explain why you accepted it.

blocks.heading: Risk and Mitigation
blocks.body: Identify what could fail: data volumes, integration outages, adoption, governance. Say how you would handle each.

blocks.heading: Speak to the Business
blocks.body: Judges assess whether a business audience could follow you. Lead with the outcome, then the mechanism.

blocks.heading: Practise Out Loud
blocks.body: Mock boards with people who interrupt are the single most useful preparation. Silent reading does not build this skill.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: The two credentials you need before CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: Which two credentials must be active before you can pursue CTA?
options: Administrator and Advanced Administrator
Sales Cloud Consultant and Service Cloud Consultant
Application Architect and System Architect
Platform Developer II and JavaScript Developer I
sampleQuestions.explanation: CTA requires both role-based architect credentials, which between them cover seven distinct exams.
whyWrong: Administrator credentials do not lead to CTA.
Consultant credentials are a different track.
Those are developer-track credentials and are not CTA prerequisites.

sampleQuestions.question: How is the CTA credential assessed?
options: By designing a solution to a scenario and defending it to judges
By completing Trailhead superbadges only
By submitting a portfolio of past projects
By a 60-question multiple-choice exam
sampleQuestions.explanation: CTA uses a scenario-based assessment with a live defence, not a multiple-choice test.
whyWrong: Superbadges are not how CTA is assessed.
You present a solution to a given scenario rather than past work.
There is no multiple-choice CTA exam.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate's design is technically elegant but does not address two business requirements stated in the scenario. What is the likely outcome?
options: It passes, because the design is technically strong
It is deferred for a written follow-up
The judges rewrite the requirements
It fails, because requirement coverage is fundamental
sampleQuestions.explanation: The board checks that the design answers the scenario. Unaddressed requirements are one of the most common reasons for failing.
whyWrong: Technical elegance does not compensate for missing the brief.
There is no written follow-up to rescue missed requirements.
The scenario is fixed; the candidate must work to it.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the architect evaluation stage?
options: To check readiness before access to the full review board
To award the CTA credential directly
To replace the Application Architect credential
To test coding ability in Apex
sampleQuestions.explanation: The evaluation is a readiness assessment that gates access to the review board.
whyWrong: The credential is awarded after the review board, not this stage.
It does not replace any prerequisite credential.
It assesses architecture judgement, not coding.

sampleQuestions.question: During questioning, a judge challenges a candidate's choice of middleware. What is the strongest response?
options: State that it is best practice
Say the client insisted on it
Explain why it was chosen, what was rejected, and the trade-off accepted
Immediately replace it with a direct integration
sampleQuestions.explanation: Judges are assessing reasoning. A justified choice with a named alternative and an acknowledged cost is what they are looking for.
whyWrong: Calling something best practice is not a justification for this scenario.
Deferring to an unnamed client does not explain the architecture.
Abandoning a decision under the first challenge suggests it was not reasoned.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best describes what the judges assess?
options: The visual polish of the slides
Judgement: requirement coverage, justification, trade-offs, risk and communication
Speed of typing a solution
Recall of Salesforce feature names
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform knowledge is assumed. The assessment is about the reasoning applied on top of it.
whyWrong: Clear diagrams help, but polish is not the criterion.
There is no typing element.
Feature recall is tested by the prerequisite exams, not the board.

sampleQuestions.question: How many distinct exams must be passed before CTA, given the two prerequisite credentials?
options: Seven, because Platform Developer I counts toward both
Eight, with no overlap between the two paths
Four, one per architect domain
Two, one for each prerequisite credential
sampleQuestions.explanation: Each credential needs four exams, and Platform Developer I appears in both, so seven are distinct.
whyWrong: There is an overlap, so it is not eight.
Four would cover only one of the two credentials.
Each prerequisite is itself made up of four exams.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate can explain their design fluently to other architects but loses the business stakeholders in the room. Why does this matter at the board?
options: It only affects the evaluation stage
It affects the fee, not the result
It does not matter, as judges are all architects
Communication to a business audience is part of what is assessed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Judges assess whether the solution can be explained to the people who would fund and use it.
whyWrong: It applies at both stages.
Fees are unrelated to performance.
Judges assess communication even though they are technical.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the most effective form of CTA preparation?
options: Watching recorded presentations without presenting
Mock boards where people interrupt and challenge the design
Memorising governor limits
Re-reading the architect exam guides
sampleQuestions.explanation: The format tests defending a design live, which can only be practised by doing it under challenge.
whyWrong: Watching builds familiarity but not the skill being tested.
Limits are assumed knowledge, not the assessed skill.
The guides cover the prerequisite exams, not this format.

sampleQuestions.question: Roughly what should a candidate budget for the two CTA stages?
options: The same as a standard $200 exam
Around US$6,000 in total, subject to confirmation with Salesforce
A fixed annual subscription
Nothing, as it is included with the prerequisites
sampleQuestions.explanation: Third-party sources put the two stages at roughly $6,000 combined. Fees change, so confirm with Salesforce before committing.
whyWrong: It costs far more than a standard exam.
It is charged per attempt, not as a subscription.
The prerequisites are paid for separately and do not include the board.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate presents a design with no stated risks, saying every requirement is fully met. How is this likely to be received?
options: Well, provided the diagram is detailed
Poorly, because every design carries trade-offs the board expects you to name
Well, because confidence is the main criterion
Neutrally, as risk is assessed separately
sampleQuestions.explanation: Claiming a design has no downsides suggests the candidate has not analysed it. Naming risks and mitigations is expected.
whyWrong: Diagram detail does not substitute for risk analysis.
Unsupported confidence is not what is assessed.
Risk is part of the same assessment, not a separate one.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement about the review board scenario is correct?
options: It is a live production org to configure
It is the candidate's own past project
It is a hypothetical enterprise scenario with requirements and constraints
It is a set of multiple-choice questions
sampleQuestions.explanation: Candidates design a solution for a hypothetical company described in the scenario.
whyWrong: There is no hands-on configuration.
Past projects are not the basis of the assessment.
There are no multiple-choice questions at the board.

sampleQuestions.question: Why is having a repeatable presentation structure useful at the board?
options: It guarantees a pass regardless of content
It replaces the need for a diagram
It lets you skip the questioning section
It ensures every required area is covered under time pressure
sampleQuestions.explanation: A set structure covering data, security, integration, lifecycle and licensing means nothing is forgotten when time is short.
whyWrong: Structure helps delivery, but the content still has to be right.
Diagrams remain central to the presentation.
Questioning follows the presentation regardless.

sampleQuestions.question: Which prerequisite exam counts toward both Application Architect and System Architect?
options: Data Architect
Integration Architect
Platform Developer I
Sharing and Visibility Architect
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform Developer I appears in both credentials, which is why seven distinct exams cover both.
whyWrong: Data Architect counts toward Application Architect only.
Integration Architect counts toward System Architect only.
Sharing and Visibility Architect counts toward Application Architect only.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate fails the board. What is the usual next step?
options: Prepare and sit the board again, paying the fee for that attempt
They are awarded a lower credential instead
They must retake all seven prerequisite exams
The credential is permanently closed to them
sampleQuestions.explanation: Candidates can reattempt, paying for each sitting. Sources differ on retake pricing, so check with Salesforce.
whyWrong: There is no consolation credential.
Active prerequisites do not need retaking.
A failure does not permanently bar a candidate.

expertInsight: CTA is not an exam you can revise your way through. The judges are not checking whether you know a feature exists; they are checking whether you can choose between two reasonable options under time pressure and say why. The people who fail usually know the platform well but cannot defend a decision, or they design something clever that does not answer the business requirement they were given. Practise out loud, in front of people who will interrupt you.
